title: Supreme Court Says No to Trump's Mail Ballot Limits
summary:
Imagine you're about to mail a letter — but suddenly someone says you have to use a brand-new envelope, and if you don't, your letter won't be delivered. That's kind of what almost happened to millions of voters in America.

On Monday, the Supreme Court said no to President Donald Trump's plan to restrict mail ballots before the midterm elections in November. The court's decision means states can keep using the same mail voting systems they've used for years. Mail ballots make up nearly one-third of all votes cast in the U.S.

Trump wanted a uniform envelope style and a new online system where states would submit lists of eligible voters. If states didn't follow the rules, the Postal Service could refuse to deliver their ballots. But a whistleblower report warned that millions of ballots might never get sent because the online portal wasn't built properly.

Two justices, Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas, disagreed with the court's decision. Alito wrote that the Postal Service has broad authority over the mail.

Election officials in states like Washington and Oregon — where all voting happens by mail — were relieved. Washington Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said the work continues "without having to upend our election processes." Colorado's Secretary of State Jena Griswold called it "a major victory for Colorado and American democracy."

The White House didn't respond to requests for comment. The court didn't explain its full reasoning, which is common for emergency decisions.
why_it_matters: You can't vote yet, but the rules about how grown-ups vote decide who runs your town, your schools and your parks — and this case shows that courts can step in when a change might stop people's votes from counting.

questions.question: What did the Supreme Court decide on Monday?
options: It closed the Postal Service for a week.
It said states must delay the midterm elections.
It said no to Trump's plan to restrict mail ballots.
It ordered everyone to vote by mail.
questions.correct_answer: It said no to Trump's plan to restrict mail ballots.

Stop letting people vote by mail in cities

background_read: The Supreme Court (the highest court in the United States, made up of nine justices whose decisions are final) decided this case quickly, without explaining all of its reasons.
Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025) asked the court to step in before the November midterm elections, when voters choose members of Congress.
A few states, like Washington and Oregon, run all their elections by mail — voters get a ballot at home, fill it out, and send it back or drop it off.
Article_Structure: WHO: The Supreme Court, President Donald Trump, two disagreeing justices (Samuel Alito and Clarence Thomas), and election officials in Washington, Oregon and Colorado.
WHAT: The court said no to Trump's plan to restrict mail ballots before the November midterm elections, so states can keep their same mail voting systems.
WHERE: Across the United States, with all-mail voting states Washington and Oregon and Colorado's secretary of state speaking about the decision.
WHY: Mail ballots are nearly one-third of all U.S. votes, and a whistleblower warned that millions of ballots might never be delivered because the new online portal was not built properly.

perspectives.description: They say states should keep using the voting systems they already have, because changing the rules right before an election could confuse voters and election workers.

Justices Alito and Thomas think the Postal Service has broad power over the mail, and some people worry that mail voting is easier to cheat with — though studies have found cheating in mail voting is very rare.

Officials in Washington, Oregon and Colorado are relieved that they can keep counting ballots the way they always have, without a last-minute scramble to buy new envelopes or build new computer systems.
